Wake up after a while, and look around to see what caused it, and maybe find a steamboat coughing her way up-stream, so far over towards the opposite shore you couldn't make out anything about her except whether she had a stern-wheel or side-wheels; then for an hour or so there wouldn't be a thing to hear or see—nothing but pure lonesomeness. After that you'd notice a raft drifting past, far off yonder, and maybe some galoot aboard chopping, because on a raft they're nearly always at it; you'd watch the axe glitter and drop—you don't hear a thing; you watch it rise once more, and just when it gets above the fellow's head you hear the k'chunk!—it had needed all that while to travel across the water. That was how we spent the day, loafing about and listening to the quiet. One time a heavy fog came, and the rafts and other things passing kept banging tin pans so the steamboats wouldn't run them down. A scow or raft passed so near we heard the people talking and swearing and laughing—as plain as anything; but we couldn't see a trace of them; it gave you a crawly feeling, like spirits behaving that way up in the air. Jim said he reckoned they were spirits; but I says:

“No; spirits wouldn't say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

As soon as night came we pushed off; after we got her pretty near the middle we left her be, and let her drift wherever the current chose to take her; then we lighted our pipes, hung our legs over in the water, and talked about every sort of thing—we went naked all day and night whenever the mosquitoes allowed it—the new clothes Buck's people had made me was too fine to feel easy in, and anyway I never thought much of clothes.

Sometimes we'd have the entire river to ourselves for a mighty long spell. Across the water lay the banks and islands; and maybe there'd be a little spark—a candle at some cabin window; and sometimes you'd see a spark or two out on the water—aboard a raft or scow, you understand; and perhaps hear a fiddle or somebody singing over on one of those crafts. Living on a raft is lovely. There was the sky overhead, all sprinkled with stars, and we'd lie on our backs looking up and talking over whether somebody made them or they just happened. Jim reckoned they was made, but I reckoned they happened; I figured making that many would have taken too long.

The studio was full of the rich fragrance of roses, and whenever the gentle summer breeze moved through the garden trees, the open doorway admitted the heavy scent of lilacs or the subtler perfume of pink hawthorn blossoms.

From his corner of the divan, made of Persian saddlebags, Lord Henry Wotton lay smoking his usual endless cigarettes. He could just glimpse the shining blossoms of a laburnum, as sweet and golden as honey, whose quivering branches seemed scarcely strong enough to support their flame-like beauty. Now and then the strange shadows of flying birds swept over the long curtains of tussore silk stretched across the enormous window. For an instant they created a Japanese effect, reminding him of those pale, jade-faced painters in Tokyo who try to suggest speed and movement through an art that must itself remain still. The low, sulky drone of bees forcing their way through the tall, uncut grass, or persistently circling the dusty golden trumpets of the sprawling honeysuckle, seemed to deepen the oppressive quiet. London's muted roar sounded like the low drone of a distant organ.

At the center of the room, fastened to an upright easel, stood a full-length portrait of an exceptionally beautiful young man. Sitting a little way in front of it was the painter himself, Basil Hallward, whose abrupt disappearance some years earlier had caused such public excitement at the time and prompted so many strange theories.

As the artist looked at the graceful, handsome figure he had captured so skillfully in his painting, a pleased smile crossed his face and seemed ready to stay. Suddenly, though, he sprang up, shut his eyes, and pressed his fingers against his eyelids, as if trying to hold inside his mind some extraordinary dream from which he was afraid of waking.

“It's your best work, Basil, the best thing you've ever done,” Lord Henry said lazily. “You absolutely must send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is too big and too vulgar. Every time I've been there, either there have been so many people I couldn't see the paintings, which was dreadful, or so many paintings I couldn't see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor really is the only place for it.”

“I don't think I'll send it anywhere,” he replied, throwing his head back in that peculiar way that used to make his friends laugh at him when he was at Oxford.

But it hardly matters.”

“I could just as well ask,” she replied, “why you told me you liked me against your will, against your judgment, and even against your character, when you so clearly meant to offend and insult me. Didn't that give me some excuse for being rude, if I was rude? But I have other reasons to be angry. You know I do. Even if my own feelings hadn't already turned against you, if I had felt nothing, or even liked you, do you think anything could persuade me to accept a man who has destroyed, perhaps forever, the happiness of a sister I love so dearly?”

At these words, Mr. Darcy's face changed color. But the emotion quickly passed, and he made no attempt to interrupt as she went on:

“I have every reason to think badly of you. Nothing can excuse your unfair and unkind behavior in that affair. You dare not deny—you cannot deny—that you were chiefly, if not entirely, responsible for separating them. You have left one open to criticism for being changeable and unreliable, and the other open to ridicule for hopes that came to nothing. You have made them both deeply miserable.”

She stopped. To her great anger, she saw that he was listening without the slightest sign of regret. He even looked at her with a smile that pretended disbelief.

“Can you deny you did this?” she asked again.

He answered with an appearance of calm. “I have no wish to deny that I did everything I could to separate my friend from your sister, or that I'm glad I succeeded. I have been kinder to him than to myself.”

Elizabeth refused to show that she had noticed this polite remark, but she understood its meaning, and it did nothing to soften her feelings.

“But that affair isn't the only reason I dislike you,” she continued. “I had formed my opinion of you long before it happened. Mr. Wickham showed me your true character in the story he told me many months ago. What can you say about that? What supposed act of friendship can you claim in your defense there? What false account can you give to mislead other people?”

“You take a keen interest in that gentleman's affairs,” Darcy said, his voice less calm and his face growing redder.

“How could anyone who knows what he has suffered help taking an interest in him?”

“What he has suffered!” Darcy repeated scornfully. “Yes, his misfortunes have been very great indeed.”

“And you caused them,” Elizabeth cried fiercely. “You have brought him to the poverty he lives in now—poverty compared with what he should have had.
